title: Mussat v. IQVIA, Inc. (2020)
summary: The Seventh Circuit declined to require separate forum contacts for each absent member of the federal statutory class.
notes:
This is a Seventh Circuit holding about a nationwide federal statutory class action. The casebook presents the broader issue as unsettled at its publication; do not label this a Supreme Court resolution. TransUnion concerns the separate Article III injury requirement.

Dr. Florence Mussat, an Illinois physician, sued under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act over two unsolicited junk faxes lacking the required opt-out notice from IQVIA (a Delaware corporation headquartered in Pennsylvania); the Seventh Circuit reasoned that 'absent class members are not full parties to the case' for personal-jurisdiction purposes, and the Supreme Court later denied certiorari.

sections.Parties: Mussat, an Illinois plaintiff, sued IQVIA, a Delaware corporation headquartered in Pennsylvania, under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act.
sections.Material Facts: The plaintiff filed in federal court in Illinois and sought a nationwide class. IQVIA was not at home in Illinois. It argued that Bristol-Myers Squibb required a forum connection for each absent class member’s claim, which would eliminate the out-of-state portion of the proposed class.
sections.Procedural History: The district court struck the nationwide class allegations. The Seventh Circuit accepted an interlocutory appeal and reversed.
sections.Issue: Did Bristol-Myers require each absent class member to establish an individual specific-jurisdiction connection in this federal statutory class action?
sections.Holding: No under the Seventh Circuit’s holding. The named representatives had to establish jurisdiction, but the unnamed class members did not each have to make that separate showing.
sections.Reasoning: The court distinguished a mass action in which every claimant is a named party from a Rule 23 representative action. Absent class members are treated as parties for some purposes and not others, and the safeguards of certification are important to that distinction. The court compared treatment of absentees in diversity and venue analysis and emphasized that Bristol-Myers had reserved questions concerning federal courts and class actions. It therefore rejected an automatic extension of that case to the posture before it.

learning.why: The Seventh Circuit declined to require separate forum contacts for each absent member of the federal statutory class.

topics.cp-absent-plaintiffs: The Seventh Circuit distinguished unnamed class members from named plaintiffs in a mass action.
topics.specific-jurisdiction: The named representative needed a sufficient jurisdictional connection, while each absentee did not need a separate showing under this holding.
topics.cp-joinder-class-distinction: The representative structure of Rule 23 distinguished the case from Bristol-Myers Squibb.
topics.cp-class-jurisdiction: The case squarely addresses personal jurisdiction in representative litigation after Bristol-Myers Squibb.
topics.cp-party-status: The holding turns on absent class members not being full parties for jurisdictional purposes.
